Su origen musical se discute: Mairena los tenía por cante básico gitano; los estudios recientes los llevan a Cuba y las habaneras llegadas a Sevilla y Cádiz en la segunda mitad del XIX; los granadinos defienden una raíz morisca (el disco Granada canta por tangos recoge trece estilos, entre ellos los de la morería). Manuel Ríos Ruiz concluye que no se sabe con certeza. La Niña de los Peines se hizo inmortal con su copla «Péinate tú con mis peines». Del tango nacen los tientos, más pausados y solemnes, que cantaron primero el Mellizo y el Marrurro y se popularizaron a comienzos del XX, y la mariana, que difundió Bernardo el de los Lobitos y hoy casi solo canta Pepe Menese con letras de Moreno Galván.

scenes.name: Las soleares
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: La madre del cante y uno de sus pilares, independiente de cualquier otro ritmo; los cantaores la consideran «el toro bravo del arte jondo». Coplas solemnes y sentenciosas de tres o cuatro octosílabos, unidas por la guitarra, que suelen rematarse por bulerías; muy apropiadas para el baile de mujer. Se desarrolló al sur del Guadalquivir desde los jaleos festivos: la primera mención es de la Andonda en Triana hacia 1840, una cantaora temible contemporánea del Fillo, y tomó su forma actual entre 1875 y 1915. Las mujeres fueron clave en su creación y transmisión (la Andonda, Mercedes la Serneta, Fernanda de Utrera, Carmen Linares). Hay soleares de Triana (la Andonda, Silverio, Fernando el de Triana, la Niña de los Peines, Tomás Pavón, Mairena), de Alcalá, más solemnes (Joaquín el de la Paula, Juan Talega), de Utrera (la Serneta, el Pinini, María Peña, Fernanda), de Cádiz y el Puerto, más jondas (Enrique Butrón, el Mellizo, Paquirri el Guanté), de Jerez, breves y llenas de melismas (Curro Frijones, José Illanda, Juan Mojama, Tío José de Paula, Manuel Torre) y de Córdoba, más pausadas.

scenes.name: Las siguiriyas, livianas y serranas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Una de las expresiones más dramáticas y de los palos más importantes: sin siguiriyas y soleares el flamenco no sería lo que es. Un quejío entero de lamentos que no admite medias tintas («con las siguiriyas no se puede vender la burra»), con coplas trágicas de cuatro versos (6, 6, 10 y 6 sílabas), muchas sobre la muerte de los seres queridos, y falsetas lentas que suenan a campanas a muerto. Lorca la describió como un grito terrible que divide el paisaje en dos; Tía Anica la Piriñaca decía que cuando la cantaba a gusto la boca le sabía a sangre. La cantaban ya el Planeta (la de la Luna, la más antigua conocida) y el Fillo; luego Manuel Torre, Silverio, Paco la Luz, Cagancho, el Nitri, Curro Dulce, el Loco Mateo, el Mellizo, Terremoto de Jerez (que cantó toda la noche por siguiriyas con su madre muerta en brazos) y Juan Talega; hoy el Chocolate y José Menese. Antonio Mairena grabó unas cuarenta y cinco formas: es el siguiriyero más importante. Sus escuelas son Jerez y los Puertos, Cádiz y Triana. En el baile la difundió Vicente Escudero y Pilar López le añadió los palillos. La liviana, cante de campo, caminos y bandoleros, prepara la voz para la serrana, a la que Silverio dio brillo y con la que se remata por siguiriyas.

scenes.name: La caña, el polo y la petenera
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Tres cantes de la familia de la soleá. La caña, con ayes más arrastrados, se sitúa en la serranía de Ronda (un viajero inglés la oyó allí en 1830) o en la voz árabe gaunia, «canción»; la cantaron el Fillo, Tío José el Granaíno, Antonio Chacón, Pepe de la Matrona y Rafael Romero el Gallina, y hoy se usa más para el baile solemne. El polo se cantaba tras la caña, con la misma métrica; el de Tobalo, su supuesto creador, aparece ya en Estébanez Calderón y hoy se usa en la soleá apolá; Enrique Morente grabó el de Chacón. La petenera, melancólica y de origen incierto, se atribuye a una mujer de Paterna de la Ribera, «la perdición de los hombres», o a los sefardíes de los Balcanes; los gitanos la evitaron porque traía mala suerte. La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: Kurt Cobain Possibly Contributed Guitar and Vocals to Hole's "Asking For It" (1993, Rio)
facts.body: An unofficial version of Hole's "Asking For It" exists featuring a male voice on background vocals widely attributed to Kurt Cobain. It is believed to have been recorded at Ariola Studios in Rio de Janeiro in January 1993 when Nirvana was there for four days and Courtney Love was traveling with the band. The version did not appear on *Live Through This*. An official outtake from the same Rio sessions, a demo of "Miss World," appears on *My Body the Hand Grenade*. "It's not that big a leap to assume that the version of asking for it was also recorded during the Rio sessions."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Nirvana

facts.title: Rio de Janeiro Studio Sessions with Hole (1993)
facts.body: From January 19th to 22nd, 1993, all three members of Nirvana engaged in studio sessions in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, to develop new material for their *In Utero* album. Courtney Love and Hole's drummer, Patty Schemel, were also present during these four days, where approximately a dozen songs were committed to tape. Given Hole's bassist was absent, the situation makes an actual Nirvana-Hole collaborative venture "fairly reasonable" to assume, especially regarding Kurt Cobain's rumored involvement on Hole's "Miss World" demo and an unreleased version of "Asking For It."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Nirvana

facts.title: Quieter Evolution (1993)
facts.body: By late 1993, Nirvana, particularly evidenced by their *MTV Unplugged* set, began to explore a quieter, more acoustic sound. This shift indicated a broader mutation within alternative rock, moving away from the heavier sounds of earlier grunge toward more subdued and melodic approaches. "Like Nirvana, on their MTV Unplugged set, we're getting quieter, more acoustic."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: A Little Love and Some Tenderness Edition Part 1
facts.name: Nirvana

facts.title: Late 1993 State of Collapse
facts.body: By late 1993, when Nirvana finally agreed to the MTV Unplugged session, the band was "completely devastated, exhausted, without energy, and on the verge of collapse." This was a stark contrast to their energetic and ambitious state in early 1993 during the recording of *In Utero*. "la propia banda llega a finales en 1993 completamente arrasada agotada sin energía y al bordo del colapso."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Por qué el MTV Unplugged de Nirvana NO es un mal álbum
facts.name: Nirvana

facts.title: Decline During 1993
facts.body: The band's degradation throughout 1993 was attributed not only to Curcomen's drug addiction but also to the exploitative practices of their label, Geffen Records, which pressured them for commercial gain. Recordings from their *In Utero* tour show a band that had lost much of its "spark" and "energy." "la degeneración de Nirvana en esa época fue fruto de muchas cosas no solo de la droga adición de curcoven."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Por qué el MTV Unplugged de Nirvana NO es un mal álbum

facts.title: Noel Gallagher's "Coup d'Etat" (Spring 1993)
facts.body: In the spring of 1993, after being fired from his job as a guitar roadie with the Inspiral Carpets and left with only £2,000 in severance pay, Noel Gallagher was determined to forge a proper music career. While impressed by his younger brother Liam's band, he offered to join on the strict condition, effectively a "coup d'etat," that he be "in charge of everything" within the group. "I will join your group, he said, but you have to let me be in charge of everything."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Forced Performance and Record Deal at King Tuts Wawa Hut (May 31, 1993)
facts.body: On Sunday, May 31, 1993, Oasis, who were not scheduled to play, physically "bullied their way on stage" for a set at King Tuts Wawa Hut in Glasgow, Scotland. Having hitched a ride with another Manchester group, 18 Wheeler, they threatened the venue's owner and bouncers with burning down the club if they weren't allowed to perform. Coincidentally, Alan McGee of Creation Records was present, initially to see other bands on the bill, but was so impressed by Oasis that he signed them "more or less on the spot," later lending them £1,000 for equipment. "Oasis literally bullied their way on stage for a set at King Tuts Wawa Hut in Glasgow, Scotland."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 7
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Discovery at King Tut's Wah Wah Hut (1993)
facts.body: On May 31, 1993, Oasis, referred to as "a bunch of Yabo's from Manchester," performed an unscheduled four-song set at King Tut's Wah Wah Hut in Glasgow. Alan McGee, head of Creation Records, was in the audience due to a mix-up in set times and, after hearing only those four songs, immediately offered them a deal with his indie label. "a bunch of Yabo's from Manchester who bullied their way on stage at a venue called King Tuts Wawa Hut in Glasgow. That was May 31, 1993. They played four songs, and in the audience that night was Alan McGee, the head of creation records. All it took though was those four songs. He offered them a deal with creation, an indie label."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Early Career (Early 1993)
facts.body: In early 1993, Oasis had played only 10 gigs and were attempting to assemble enough material for a show in Liverpool scheduled four weeks later. "A new group called Oasis had played all of 10 gigs and were trying to pull together enough material for a show in 4 weeks in Liverpool."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Record Deal Acquisition (May 31, 1993)
facts.body: Oasis secured a record deal after a show on May 31, 1993. "They still didn't have a record deal. That would come after a show on May 31, 1993."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Album Artwork Collaboration (1993-1998)
facts.body: Noel Gallagher first met designer Brian Cannon about a year before Oasis's debut album and was impressed by his work for The Verve, bonding over Adidas running shoe designs. Noel specifically requested Cannon to design Oasis's artwork once they were signed, a collaboration that continued for the next four years, covering their early albums and singles. "Telling Brian, when we get signed, I want you to do our artwork."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Rapid Ascent to Stardom (1993-1994)
facts.body: Oasis experienced an exceptionally rapid rise to fame, transitioning from unknown to superstars within months of their discovery in 1993. This swift progression contrasted sharply with bands like Pulp, Suede, and Blur, who endured years, or even a decade, of development before achieving widespread recognition. "oasis en casi unos meses de ser descubiertos a ser super estrellas no pasan casi unos meses."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Discovery by Creation Records and Sony Acquisition (1993)
facts.body: Oasis was initially discovered and championed in 1993 by Creation Records, an independent label known for breaking acts like My Bloody Valentine. Crucially, Sony acquired Creation Records precisely as Oasis's recording contract was being finalized, granting the band immediate access to the significant promotional and financial resources of Sony Music for their launch. "Sony compro clientes son recursos justo al tiempo en el que estaban firmando el contrato escoráfico de oasis."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Oasis

facts.title: Noel Gallagher's "Coup d'Etat" (Spring 1993)
facts.body: In the spring of 1993, after being fired from his job as a guitar roadie with the Inspiral Carpets and left with only £2,000 in severance pay, Noel Gallagher was determined to forge a proper music career. While impressed by his younger brother Liam's band, he offered to join on the strict condition, effectively a "coup d'etat," that he be "in charge of everything" within the group. "I will join your group, he said, but you have to let me be in charge of everything."

facts.title: Adam Clayton's Absence and Substitute Performance (1993)
facts.body: During the 1993 Zoo TV tour in Australia, bassist Adam Clayton experienced a three-day bender following a breakup, rendering him too drunk to perform at a crucial show at Sydney Football Stadium on November 26, 1993. His bass tech, Edward Morgan, stepped in to perform the entire show. "But Adam was way too drunk to be on stage. He was up to a Rody Adam's base text to Edward Morgan to fill in."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: We Are The Road Crew - A History of Roadies

facts.title: Judgment Night Soundtrack Crossover (1993)
facts.body: The 1993 *Judgment Night* soundtrack, featuring 11 collaborations between rock and hip-hop artists, was a radical concept at the time due to limited crossover between the genres. It served as a major catalyst for bringing many rock and metal fans into the hip-hop world for the first time, fostering mutual understanding and realizing shared commonalities. "But for the most part, rock and hip-hop lived in different worlds, not after Judgment Night."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: hip hop

facts.title: First Rap Diss Record in Pop Top 10 - "Dre Day" (1993)
facts.body: Dr. Dre's "Dre Day" (full title "Fuck Wit Dre Day (And Everybody's Celebratin')") became the first rap diss record to crack the pop top 10, reaching number 8 on the Hot 100 and number 6 on the R&B charts in the summer of 1993. This was a historic moment for the genre, demonstrating a growing mainstream acceptance of diss tracks. "That made Dre Day the first rap disrecord to make the pop top 10."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.name: hip hop

facts.title: Peak Popularity and Market Impact (1993)
facts.body: In October 1993, Grunge was at its absolute peak, and Pearl Jam's fanatical sales for their album "Vs." served as a "giant wake-up call" that "New Rock," "Alt Rock," "alternative music," or "modern rock" had undeniably "arrived." "Now Grunge, if you remember, was at its absolute peak and fanaticism of Pearl Jam was especially, well, fanatical."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 2
facts.name: Grunge

facts.title: Spread to Britain (Early 1993)
facts.body: In early 1993, the spread of American Grunge was causing an "operative crisis" for British music and contributing to the decline of the Manchester Sound. "British music was about to inter-operative crisis thanks to the spread of American Grunge."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Grunge

facts.title: Dave Navarro's Recruitment (September 1993)
facts.body: Dave Navarro joined the Red Hot Chili Peppers in September 1993, replacing Jesse Tobias, who had been with the band for less than a year. Navarro had been courted by several bands after Jane's Addiction disbanded, including an offer from Guns N' Roses to replace Izzy Stradlin, which he declined. Although he initially doubted his suitability for the band's funky style, he was persuaded to join. "Dave joined the Chili Peppers in September 1993 as a replacement for Jesse Tobias, who had been with the band for less than a year."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Red Hot Chili Peppers

facts.title: Decadence of the Devotional Tour (1993-1994)
facts.body: The world tour of 1993-1994, known as the "Devotional Tour," was marked by gargantuan excess and decadence, including backstage VIP areas and hotel suites "outfitted like the set of a porn movie," where parties fueled by liquid ecstasy often lasted up to three days. Allegations of S&M were made, but widespread drunkenness and drug use made reliable record-keeping difficult. "Each night up to 20 of the most beautiful women in the audience were invited into special backstage VIP areas and hotel suites that were outfitted like the set of a porn movie."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Dave Gahan and Darabomonte Arrested in Montreal (September 8, 1993)
facts.body: On September 8, 1993, Dave Gahan and touring keyboardist Darabomonte were arrested and jailed in Montreal after Dave punched a hotel concierge. This incident occurred after a loud party in their suite led to numerous complaints, prompting the hotel to cut their power. "September 8, 1993. Dave Cajon and Touring Keyboard as Darabomonte are arrested and jailed after Dave punched the concierge of a Montreal hotel in the mouth."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Martin Gore Arrested in Denver (November 4, 1993)
facts.body: On November 4, 1993, Martin Gore was arrested at the Weston Hotel in Denver. The arrest happened after he refused to turn down his stereo at 4 in the morning following complaints about the noise. "November 4, 1993. Martin Gore was arrested at the Weston Hotel in Denver after refusing to turn down the stereo at 4 in the morning."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Dave Gahan's Mid-Show Heart Attack (October 8, 1993)
facts.body: On October 8, 1993, Dave Gahan suffered a heart attack mid-show in New Orleans but remarkably managed to finish the set before being removed backstage by paramedics. "Dave is removed from backstage at a show in New Orleans by paramedics after he suffered a heart attack. He actually had a heart attack mid-show, but he somehow managed to finish the set."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Devotional Tour - Most Debauched Rock Tour Ever (1993-1994)
facts.body: The tour promoting "Songs of Faith and Devotion" lasted eight months, featuring extreme alcohol and drug use that led to members suffering heart attacks, seizures, severe mental illness, and an overdose that left one member clinically dead for two minutes. It employed 100 people, including a full-time psychiatrist, and a dedicated drug sourcer. "It has gone down in history, as the most debauched rock tour ever."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Devotional Tour Logistics (1993)
facts.body: The initial plan for the Devotional Tour was ambitious, encompassing 158 dates across 27 countries, covering approximately 100,000 miles. It required almost 100 tons of equipment and featured a stage designed by photographer and artist Anton Corbijn, who was undertaking such a design for the first time. "The initial plan was for 158 dates through 27 countries covering about 100,000 miles and requiring almost 100 tons of equipment with a stage designed by photographer and artist Anton Corbin, something that he'd never done before."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Devotional Tour European Leg (May 19 – July 31, 1993)
facts.body: The Devotional Tour kicked off on May 19, 1993, in Lille, France, marking the beginning of an 11-week European leg that concluded on July 31 in London. Throughout this period, relations among the four band members remained highly strained, with significant concern focused on singer Dave Gahan. "Depeche Mode's devotional tour began on May 19, 1993 in Lil France, the start of an 11-week European tour that ended in London on July 31."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Band Isolation During Devotional Tour (1993)
facts.body: During the North American leg of the Devotional Tour, Dave Gahan's increasingly insufferable ego and "rock god" persona led the other band members to insist on staying on separate floors in hotels to manage the extreme tension. "He became so unsufferable that when it came to staying in hotels, the other members of the group insisted on being on separate floors from Dave."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Banned from Berlin's Intercontinental Hotel (June 1993)
facts.body: During the Devotional Tour's stop in Berlin in June 1993, Depeche Mode was banned from the Intercontinental Hotel, their usual accommodation, due to Dave Gahan's behavior, which included spending days injecting heroin in his room. "In June 1993, when the tour rolled into Berlin, the Pesh Mode was banned from the intercontinental hotel, which was their usual place."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Devotional Tour Vampire Phase (1993)
facts.body: Dave Gahan reportedly entered a "vampire phase" during the Devotional Tour, keeping his dressing room dark and filled with candles. As a joke, a coffin was delivered to the tour, which Dave Gahan used to take naps before each show. "There was a rumor that Dave went through a vampire phase, his dressing room was dark and filled with candles, and as a joke, someone delivered a coffin to the tour."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Primal Scream's Shocking Experience (1993)
facts.body: Dave Gahan reportedly insisted that Primal Scream open for Depeche Mode on the Devotional Tour because he knew they enjoyed partying. However, Primal Scream was so appalled by the level of drug use and excess they witnessed that they allegedly gave up drugs entirely, despite their prior extensive use. "The story goes that primal scream was so shocked by what they saw that they gave up drugs entirely."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Near-Death Plane Incident (Nov 1993)
facts.body: During a break in the Devotional Tour, a private jet chartered for the band and entourage to travel from Dallas to the Caribbean experienced a pressurization problem. The plane struggled to return to Texas, an incident that deeply unnerved everyone on board. "There was a pressurization problem in the plane struggle to get back to Texas, which freaked everybody out."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Devotional Tour Environment (1993-94)
facts.body: The Depeche Mode Devotional Tour in 1993-94 was marked by significant debauchery, particularly from Dave Gahan, which reportedly "scared straight" the opening act, Primal Scream. The tour environment was so intense that it featured both its own drug counselor and a drug dealer, alongside frequent run-ins with the police. "The tour had both its own drug counselor and drug dealer. There were run-ins with the cops."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Early Touring and Struggles (1993)
facts.body: Following the release of "Pablo Honey," Radiohead embarked on an extensive tour, performing "350 live shows." During this period, they faced "an uphill battle to be taken seriously" by the music industry and audiences. "The band started out a string of 350 live shows facing an uphill battle to be taken seriously."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Radiohead

facts.title: Drug-Induced Heart Attack and Paranoia (1993-1994)
facts.body: During the 1993 tour for "Songs of Faith and Devotion," Dave Gahan's heroin use became so severe he spent days injecting himself in hotel rooms, leading to a mild heart attack in New Orleans that prevented him from performing an encore. After the tour, he returned to LA, experiencing deep drug paranoia, carrying a gun everywhere, watching the Weather Channel for 24 hours straight, and hallucinating conversations with his stuffed animals. "Drugs had brought on a mild heart attack."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Prodigy Network Hack (Early 1993)
facts.body: In February 1993, hackers on the Prodigy computer network attempted to steal information about Depeche Mode's unreleased album, "Songs of Faith and Devotion." These hackers, limited by dial-up modems, could only obtain text files of track listings and early unpublished reviews, causing record companies to "freak out." "Hackers on an old pre-interdit computer network called Prodigy were busy trying to steal information about Depeche Mode's new album, Songs of Faith and Devotion, which wasn't scheduled for release for another month and a half."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Origin (Early 1993)
facts.body: In early 1993, Radiohead was a new band from Oxford, England, that people were starting to talk about. "People were beginning to talk about a new band from Oxford, England called Radiohead."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Radiohead

facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Devotional Tour Logistics (1993)
facts.body: The initial plan for the Devotional Tour was ambitious, encompassing 158 dates across 27 countries, covering approximately 100,000 miles. It required almost 100 tons of equipment and featured a stage designed by photographer and artist Anton Corbijn, who was undertaking such a design for the first time. "The initial plan was for 158 dates through 27 countries covering about 100,000 miles and requiring almost 100 tons of equipment with a stage designed by photographer and artist Anton Corbin, something that he'd never done before."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Devotional Tour Vampire Phase (1993)
facts.body: Dave Gahan reportedly entered a "vampire phase" during the Devotional Tour, keeping his dressing room dark and filled with candles. As a joke, a coffin was delivered to the tour, which Dave Gahan used to take naps before each show. "There was a rumor that Dave went through a vampire phase, his dressing room was dark and filled with candles, and as a joke, someone delivered a coffin to the tour."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Drug-Induced Heart Attack and Paranoia (1993-1994)
facts.body: During the 1993 tour for "Songs of Faith and Devotion," Dave Gahan's heroin use became so severe he spent days injecting himself in hotel rooms, leading to a mild heart attack in New Orleans that prevented him from performing an encore. After the tour, he returned to LA, experiencing deep drug paranoia, carrying a gun everywhere, watching the Weather Channel for 24 hours straight, and hallucinating conversations with his stuffed animals. "Drugs had brought on a mild heart attack."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Martin Gore Arrested in Denver (November 4, 1993)
facts.body: On November 4, 1993, Martin Gore was arrested at the Weston Hotel in Denver. The arrest happened after he refused to turn down his stereo at 4 in the morning following complaints about the noise. "November 4, 1993. Martin Gore was arrested at the Weston Hotel in Denver after refusing to turn down the stereo at 4 in the morning."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Near-Death Plane Incident (Nov 1993)
facts.body: During a break in the Devotional Tour, a private jet chartered for the band and entourage to travel from Dallas to the Caribbean experienced a pressurization problem. The plane struggled to return to Texas, an incident that deeply unnerved everyone on board. "There was a pressurization problem in the plane struggle to get back to Texas, which freaked everybody out."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Prodigy Network Hack (Early 1993)
facts.body: In February 1993, hackers on the Prodigy computer network attempted to steal information about Depeche Mode's unreleased album, "Songs of Faith and Devotion." These hackers, limited by dial-up modems, could only obtain text files of track listings and early unpublished reviews, causing record companies to "freak out." "Hackers on an old pre-interdit computer network called Prodigy were busy trying to steal information about Depeche Mode's new album, Songs of Faith and Devotion, which wasn't scheduled for release for another month and a half."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: Early Touring and Struggles (1993)
facts.body: Following the release of "Pablo Honey," Radiohead embarked on an extensive tour, performing "350 live shows." During this period, they faced "an uphill battle to be taken seriously" by the music industry and audiences. "The band started out a string of 350 live shows facing an uphill battle to be taken seriously."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Radiohead

facts.title: Origin (Early 1993)
facts.body: In early 1993, Radiohead was a new band from Oxford, England, that people were starting to talk about. "People were beginning to talk about a new band from Oxford, England called Radiohead."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Radiohead

facts.title: Hotel Room Destruction (December 1993)
facts.body: In December 1993, Kurt Cobain and Nirvana destroyed a hotel room in St. Paul, Minnesota, while "really, really drunk." The damage amounted to $19,000 at the time, equivalent to about $37,000 today. "In December 1993, Nirvana destroyed a hotel room in St. Paul, Minnesota."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: May 9, 1993 Overdose
facts.body: Kurt was rescued from an overdose on May 9, 1993, when paramedics administered a shot of Narcan just in time. This was not an isolated incident, as he overdosed almost a dozen times in the last ten months of his life. "On May 9, 1993, he was rescued from an overdose when paramedics gave him a shot of narcan just in time."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: June 1993 Gun Call
facts.body: Police were called to Kurt's home on Lake Washington Boulevard in June 1993 to diffuse a situation involving a gun. "There was a gun call to the home on Lake Washington Boulevard in June 1993."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: Ongoing Stomach Pain Issues (1993-1994)
facts.body: For six months leading up to his death, Kurt Cobain suffered from severe stomach pain, for which he consulted nine different specialists on both coasts. Crohn's disease and IBS were ruled out, with possibilities including a severe form of acid reflux or a pinched nerve, which could explain why opioids temporarily relieved his pain. His personal journals extensively documented these struggles, including a desire to have a disease named after him and to create a rock opera about his gastric issues. "Let me just have my own very unexplainable rare stomach disease named after me."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: Opioid Prescriptions and Self-Medication (1993-1994)
facts.body: In an attempt to manage his chronic stomach pain, Kurt Cobain was prescribed various opioids, including Percodan, morphine, and bupranex, which provided temporary relief. However, he also engaged in self-medication with heroin, a habit that led to multiple overdose incidents in the final months of his life. "Perkadan and morphine were prescribed. If you go back through the scrolls and Kurt's now famous personal journals, you'll find many entries about a stomach."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: Frequent Heroin Overdoses (1993-1994)
facts.body: Kurt Cobain experienced numerous heroin overdoses, with nearly a dozen occurring in the ten months before his death. Notable incidents include an overdose on May 3, 1993, after injecting between $30 and $40 of cheap heroin, and another on May 9, 1993, from which paramedics rescued him with Narcan. A further overdose occurred in a New York hotel bathroom on July 23, 1993. "In the last 10 months of his life, Kurt Cobain OD'd almost a dozen times."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: Isolation and "Rapunzel" Nickname (1993-1994)
facts.body: Due to his increasing isolation and drug use, Kurt Cobain's friends began to refer to him as "Rapunzel," reflecting his tendency to rarely leave his room. This period of withdrawal contributed to concerns about his worsening depression and overall well-being. "He was so isolated that his friends began calling him Rapunzel because he rarely came down from his room."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: Domestic Disputes and Police Involvement (1993-1994)
facts.body: Kurt Cobain's turbulent relationship with Courtney Love led to several police interventions. On June 4, 1993, police were called to their Lake Washington Boulevard home to de-escalate a domestic situation, though charges were later dropped. On March 18, 1994, officers were again summoned after Kurt locked himself in a room with guns and threatened suicide, resulting in the confiscation of four firearms and 25 boxes of ammunition. "There was a police call to his home on Lake Washington Boulevard on June 4th, 1993."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: Suicidal Ideation and Depression (1993-1994)
facts.body: Following an overdose in July 1993, Kurt Cobain confessed in an interview with the British magazine The Face that he had "always been suicidal." His depression deepened in the fall of 1993, when he was frequently described as "strung out" and "semi-conscious." On legal documents related to a new book about Nirvana, he even listed his address as "hell on earth," underscoring his profound mental distress. "In the days after, he gave an interview to the British magazine The Face, where he convinced I've always been suicidal."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: Obsession with His Will and Financial Conflicts (1993-1994)
facts.body: In the period leading up to his death, Kurt Cobain became increasingly preoccupied with writing his will, a concern noted by a nanny working in his house. This obsession coincided with significant financial disputes within Nirvana, as Kurt demanded a larger share of royalties and declined a $9 million Lollapalooza headline slot, further straining his relationship with bandmates and management. "And why had Kurt become so obsessed with writing his will?"
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: Alleged Nirvana Breakup Threat (September 10, 1993)
facts.body: Tom Grant's theory posited that Kurt Cobain was prepared to dissolve Nirvana and join Hole with Courtney Love, suggesting this might have provided a motive for murder. In a September 10, 1993, interview with a French TV journalist, Kurt himself expressed a desire to quit Nirvana and join Hole, citing a higher level of musical connection with Courtney, but acknowledged it was "completely unrealistic" due to public perception intertwining them. "It's a nice thought, collaborations with Courtney. I'd like to, but to tell you the truth, I would rather just quit my ban and join whole."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: Elden Hoke's Allegations of Murder-for-Hire (December 1993)
facts.body: Elden Hoke (Eldu-Cher), frontman of the punk band The Mentors, publicly claimed in a 1996 High Times interview and a 1998 documentary that Courtney Love offered him $50,000 in December 1993 to kill Kurt Cobain. Hoke stated she said, "I need you to blow my old man's head off." He recounted an exchange outside a Los Angeles record store, corroborated by the owner, and said Courtney later called for him in March 1994. Although Hoke passed a lie detector test, his claims remain unverified and are often dismissed due to his unreliable narrator status. "Eldu-Cher claimed that in December 1993, Courtney offered him $50,000 to kill her husband."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Kurt Cobain

facts.title: Another Roadside Attraction Festival (1993)
facts.body: In 1993, during a period of significant financial prosperity in the music industry, The Tragically Hip launched their own cross-Canada caravan festival called "Another Roadside Attraction." The inaugural festival featured a lineup that included Matthew Sweet, The Rheostatics, Hot House Flowers, Midnight Oil, Daniel Lanois, World Party, Ziggy Marley, and Wilco. "Back when the music industry had all kinds of money to burn, the hip stage their own cross-Canada caravan festival called another roadside attraction. The first one hit the road in 1993 and Matthew Sweet, the reostatics, hot house flowers, midnight oil, Daniel Landwine, world party, Ziggy Marley, Wilcoe and others went along for the ride."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Tragically Hip

facts.title: Another Roadside Attraction Festival (1993)
facts.body: At the peak of their powers, The Tragically Hip decided to take friends on the road for a summer tour, creating their own traveling caravan festival called "Another Roadside Attraction." This festival was staged three times: in 1993, 1995, and 1997. "Their traveling caravan was called another roadside attraction. It was staged three times, 1993, 1995, and 1997."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Tragically Hip

facts.body: The combination of Andy Warhol's death, the recognition by Václav Havel and the "Velvet Revolution," and the increasing mythology built by reissued records finally pushed the band to reunite, with their first reunion concert taking place in Edinburgh, Scotland, on June 1, 1993. facts.title: Judgment Night Collaboration with Cypress Hill (1993)
facts.body: Pearl Jam collaborated with hip-hop outfit Cypress Hill for the 1993 *Judgment Night* soundtrack. This pairing was considered radical at the time due to the limited crossover between rock and hip-hop. The project was a major catalyst for the creation of rap rock and nu metal, and helped bridge the divide between rock and hip-hop fans. "The pairings included Pearl Jam and Cypress Hill, Slayer working with Ice Tea, Faith No More and Buella Tribe, Dinosaur Jr., and Del the Funky Homo sapien, 11 collaborations at all."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Eddie Vedder at Rock for Choice (February 1993)
facts.body: In February 1993, Eddie Vedder of Pearl Jam returned from Los Angeles after participating in a "Rock for Choice" concert. "Eddie Vetter of Pearl Jam arrived home from LA where he just participated in a rock for choice concert."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Pearl Jam

facts.title: Biggest Band on Charts (1993)
facts.body: By 1993, Pearl Jam had established themselves as arguably the biggest band on the charts. Their immense popularity set a high benchmark against which other bands, including Hootie & the Blowfish, were often compared, particularly regarding the power and passion of their lead singer, Eddie Vedder. "Eddie Vetter, the lead singer of Pearl Jam, who by 1993 were basically the biggest band on the charts."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.title: British Market Receptiveness (1993)
facts.body: In 1993, the British music market was experiencing a powerful surge, creating an exceptionally receptive environment for new bands. This strong momentum, fueled by existing acts like Blur and Suede, was a critical factor in the rapid and successful emergence of groups like Oasis. "El mercado musical británico como a final de 1993 era ser evidente, me refiero con Blur, con suade, con muchas cosas que ya estaban embujando muy fuerte."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.name: Britpop

facts.title: Official Start (April 1993)
facts.body: Some British texts and articles suggest that the Britpop movement officially began with Suede's cover story in SELECT magazine in April 1993, coinciding with the release of their debut album. "el ripop empiezo oficialmente con la portada de abril de 1993 en la revista SELECT."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Mental Health Struggles and Suicide Attempts (1993-2016)
facts.body: Sinead's mental health issues were public, including a denied suicide attempt involving sleeping pills in late 1993, and a definite attempt on her 33rd birthday (December 8, 1999) where she took 20 Valium pills following a custody court case involving her daughter Róisín. She was initially misdiagnosed with bipolar disorder, later receiving diagnoses of complex post-traumatic stress disorder and borderline personality disorder. In 2016, she disappeared from her Chicago suburb residence amidst rumors of a suicide attempt, but was located safely. "There was definitely a suicide attempt under 33rd birthday, which was December 8, 1999."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Sinead O'Connor

facts.title: Poor Distribution of "Black Tie White Noise" (1993)
facts.body: David Bowie's 1993 album "Black Tie White Noise" was released on a "small subsidiary of RCA Records" and suffered from poor distribution and promotion. This logistical failure contributed significantly to the album barely scraping the top 40 and becoming his shortest-lived album on the Billboard 200. "Unfortunately, Black Tie White Noise was released on a small subsidiary of RCA Records and was poorly distributed and promoted."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.name: RCA Records

facts.title: Early Career Momentum and Perception (1993)
facts.body: After their Lollapalooza 1993 performance, Rage Against the Machine was perceived as a "new, young, angry band" whose debut album and live reaction indicated they were "destined to be the biggest band in the world." However, this potential did not fully materialize as expected due to various internal and external challenges. "Their debut album was so good and the reaction to what they played and said and performed was so positive that it seemed that they were just destined to be the biggest band in the world."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Rage Against The Machine

facts.title: Alleged Murder-for-Hire Offer (1993)
facts.body: Elden Hoke (Elduchet), singer for The Mentors, claimed in the April 1996 edition of High Times Magazine that in December 1993, Courtney Love offered him $50,000 to kill her husband, Kurt Cobain. Hoke quoted her as saying, "I need you to blow my old man's head off. I'll give you $50,000 to blow his effing head off." "Courtney Love offered him $50,000 to kill her husband."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Courtney Love

facts.title: Corroborated Meeting Location (1993)
facts.body: Elden Hoke's claim about Courtney Love offering him money was partially corroborated by the owner of a record store called Rockshop on Wilcox Avenue in Los Angeles. Hoke stated Courtney pulled up in a limousine outside the store and exchanged car keys, a detail the owner confirmed. "The owner of the store corroborates Elduchet's story."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Courtney Love

facts.title: Emergence from Rave Scene Fragmentation (1993)
facts.body: Hardcore emerged around 1993 as the increasingly vast rave scene began to fracture. New subcultures within the movement demanded faster, harder, and more radical sounds, leading to the development of hardcore as a distinct and diverse branch of rave music. "De esta expresión surgió lo que pronto se conocería como hardcore, la Rave dungra narbol del que blotaría ambaya ramas diferentes."
facts.source: Central Sonora

facts.title: Undertow (1993) Hidden Audio Hoax
facts.body: The album "Undertow" features an elaborate hidden audio segment after the track "Disgustipated." This segment, which includes cricket sounds and a spoken word piece attributed to Maynard James Keenan, is part of a complex hoax crafted by Tool. It references a fictional philosopher named Ronald P. Vincent, who supposedly authored "A Joyful Guide to Lachrymology" in 1949, a non-existent study of crying and suffering that Tool falsely claimed as a philosophical guide. The band also claimed their members' ages totaled 103, a significant number for "Lachrymologists," relating to Roman tomb artifacts. This entire narrative is a deliberate red herring. "A lot of people have lost many hours studying that passage at the end of Disgustipated. And to all of you, I wish you luck because it's nothing but a TOOL hoax and a really cool dead end."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Tool

facts.title: Unceremonious Breakup via Fax (1993)
facts.body: After their U2 tour concluded in Vancouver on April 25, 1992, the band agreed to a one-year hiatus. However, on January 15, 1993, singer Black Francis unilaterally decided to leave and officially break up the band by sending a fax to their management company, a decision he later regretted. "But then on January 15, 1993, singer black france is decided that he wanted out for good. So how did he do it? Well he sent a fax to the management company saying that he was out and that the band is officially breaking up."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

facts.title: Financial Impact of "Shape of My Heart" Samples (Post-1993)
facts.body: Although "Shape of My Heart" was not a significant hit when released in 1993, its enduring appeal as a sample source, particularly for Juice Wrld's "Lucid Dreams," has generated millions of dollars. Sting shares the publishing on the song with his long-time guitarist Dominic Miller, who created the core guitar riff. "Sting has quipped in interviews that Lucid Dreams will put his grandkids through college, because it is built out of a sample of shape of my heart, a track from his lushly romantic 1993 album, Ten Summoners Tales."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: If You Love Sting, Set Him Free Edition Part 2
facts.name: Sting

facts.title: Influence on Wine Purchasing Behavior (1993)
facts.body: A 1993 experiment demonstrated that playing classical music in a wine store influenced customer behavior. Shoppers would spend more time examining wine labels and were more likely to purchase more expensive bottles compared to when other genres of music were played. "A 1993 experiment showed that when classical music was played, people stopped and examined the labels more often and more carefully when compared to times when other genres of music were playing. They also ended up buying more expensive bottles of wine."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 60 Mind-Blowing Facts About Music in 60 Minutes: 2017 Edition
facts.name: classical

facts.title: Band Formation and Longevity (1993-present)
facts.body: Billy Talent formed in 1993, with the same four core members staying together since then. This long-standing lineup is considered an exception in the music industry, comparable to bands like Radiohead, U2 (since 1978), and ZZ Top (since 1969). The band members feel their identity is deeply intertwined with the band, having started at a young age, around 17.

facts.title: Informal Dissolution (1993)
facts.body: My Bloody Valentine never officially broke up; instead, leader Kevin Shields became distracted. After the release of their expensive and groundbreaking "Loveless" album in 1991, they signed with Island Records and received a half-million-dollar advance, which was spent building a new studio. This studio proved to be "awful" with numerous technical problems. The band "just sort of evaporated" by the end of 1993, with their existence effectively ceasing around July 1, 1993. "And by the end of 1993, the band had just sort of evaporated."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2
facts.name: My Bloody Valentine

facts.title: Judgment Night Soundtrack as Catalyst (1993)
facts.body: The 1993 *Judgment Night* soundtrack, featuring unprecedented collaborations between rock and hip-hop acts, served as a major catalyst for the creation of nu metal. This project, which brought together 11 diverse pairings, helped popularize the crossover of these genres and led to the widespread success of nu metal later in the 1990s. "In retrospect, this was a major catalyst for the creation of rap rock and new metal, two genres that would be very, very big later in the decade."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Nu Metal

facts.title: Cover Story on Select Magazine - April 1993
facts.body: The April 1993 issue of Select magazine, which became a mouthpiece for Britpop, featured Suede's Brett Anderson on the cover with the headline "Yanks Go Home." This solidified their role in the burgeoning movement against American music dominance. "The April 1993 issue featured Swade's Brit Anderson on the cover next to a headline that read, Yanks Go Home."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12
facts.name: Suede

facts.title: Financial Success as an Unsigned Band (1993)
facts.body: Despite not being signed to a major label, Hootie & the Blowfish achieved remarkable financial success in 1993. They commanded between $5,000 and $10,000 per show and, combined with the 25,000 copies sold of their self-released *Kootchippop* EP, they earned over $300,000 that year. "Between that revenue and their live gigs, for which Hoody were now commanding between $5,000 and $10,000 a show, the band pulled down more than $300,000 in 1993 alone."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: A Little Love and Some Tenderness Edition Part 1
facts.name: Hootie & The Blowfish

facts.title: Discovery by Tim Summer (1993)
facts.body: Tim Summer, an A&R representative for Atlantic Records, discovered Hootie & the Blowfish at a gig in Charleston, South Carolina, in mid-September 1993. He was the only A&R person in attendance and was astonished to find a regionally popular band that was packing clubs across the Eastern Seaboard and had independently sold tens of thousands of CDs, realizing the immense potential that major labels had overlooked. "When he finally saw the band in mid-September, 1993 at a gig in Charleston, South Carolina, he was the only A&R guy in the crowd."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: A Little Love and Some Tenderness Edition Part 1
facts.name: Hootie & The Blowfish

facts.title: Major Label Release (Late 1993)
facts.body: In late 1993, after years of releasing music independently through their own label, the band was persuaded to release their next album on Atlantic Records, a major label that was part of Warner. "In late 1993, the band that founded their own label, Epitaph Records, in 1980, were themselves persuaded to release their next album on a major, Atlantic Records, who were part of Warner."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Rise in 1993
facts.body: Daniel Lanois began his rise in 1993, joining a wave of new Canadian artists gaining attention both domestically and internationally. This marked a period when foreign music fans started discovering Canadian talent. "1993, Doe Boys, the Tea Party, Daniel Landwaw, More Sarah McLaughlin, More Pursuit of Happiness, More Cowboy Junkeys."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
